marginaleffects methods for mvgam objects

Source: R/marginaleffects.mvgam.R
mvgam_marginaleffects.Rd

These methods let marginaleffects::predictions(), marginaleffects::slopes() and marginaleffects::comparisons() take an mvgam fit. get_predict() returns the posterior draws in the posterior_draws attribute. marginaleffects computes every summary from those draws. get_coef(), get_vcov() and set_coef() complete the methods marginaleffects calls. The draws carry the uncertainty. None of the three changes a result.

Prediction scale

mvgam registers three type values with marginaleffects:

  • "expected": the expectation E[Y]. Most other model classes call this "response".

  • "response": predictive draws with observation noise, on the outcome scale. A count family gives integers.

  • "link": the linear predictor.

marginaleffects takes "response" as the default. Pass type = "expected" for the expectation. comparisons() and slopes() replace "response" with "expected". A contrast differences two predictions. Observation noise in each would widen it. A slope also divides that noise by a small step. The result keeps the label "response". predictions() on "response" keeps the observation noise. marginaleffects summarises the draws by their posterior median. For a right-skewed predictive distribution the median falls below the mean.

The latent trend

With process_error = FALSE, the default, the trend contributes its deterministic submodel. Each draw keeps its own coefficients. The result is a covariate effect with the latent process held out. Its credible band excludes the uncertainty of the latent state.

A slope or comparison taken this way is biased low against the model's own E[Y]. Its expectation leaves out the trend's stationary spread. Under a log link and an AR(1) trend the factor is \(\exp(\sigma^2 / (2(1 - \rho^2)))\). process_error = TRUE gives the unbiased effect. Its band is wider because it includes the uncertainty of the latent state.

When an autoregressive process carries most of the series-level variation, a covariate effect shows little under either setting. hindcast.mvgam() and forecast.mvgam() return the state the model inferred.

References

Arel-Bundock, V., Greifer, N. and Heiss, A. (2024). How to interpret statistical models using marginaleffects for R and Python. Journal of Statistical Software, 111(9):1-32. doi:10.18637/jss.v111.i09
